title: Delhi Court Orders Swiggy, Restaurant to Pay ₹1 Lakh Over Misleading 'Cost for Two'
excerpt: The North Delhi consumer commission ruled that a "cost for two" figure shown without any disclaimer is a binding price promise — and that Swiggy can't dodge liability behind intermediary safe harbour when it does no price checks.
body:
• The District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (North Delhi) directed Swiggy and Themis Barbeque House to jointly pay ₹1 lakh as compensation, plus refunds of ₹3,988 and ₹254 — each with 9% annual interest from April 7, 2024 — after a diner was billed far above the "cost for two" shown on Swiggy Dineout.
  • The listed "cost for two" of ₹1,500 sat 40–47% below the actual buffet billing (₹1,050 vegetarian, ₹1,100 non-vegetarian per person). With no estimate or disclaimer on the listing, the bench called it a binding price promise and a misleading advertisement.
  • Swiggy's claim of intermediary protection under Section 79 of the IT Act was rejected: safe harbour needs demonstrated due diligence, and the platform showed no mechanism to reconcile displayed prices with actual bills.
  • If a restaurant bills you far above the "cost for two" shown when you booked, screenshot the listing and keep the bill: the Commission held the platform and the restaurant equally liable, so both are on the hook.

The news

A Delhi consumer court has put food-aggregator platforms on notice: the "cost for two" figure shown while booking a table is not a rough guess the platform can disown later — it is a price promise the platform shares responsibility for.

The District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission-I (North District), led by President Divya Jyoti Jaipuriar, has held Swiggy (Bundl Technologies) and Themis Barbeque House equally liable for displaying a "cost for two" of ₹1,500 on Swiggy Dineout and then billing substantially more. The two were directed to pay ₹1 lakh jointly as compensation for mental agony, harassment, inconvenience and litigation costs, according to LiveLaw.

The restaurant must also refund ₹3,988 — the excess charged over the represented price — and ₹254 toward a service charge on beverages, both with 9% annual interest from April 7, 2024, the date of the meal. If unpaid within four weeks of receiving the order, 12% annual interest applies on the entire sum.

Context & background

Complainant Praveen Kumar Singh booked tables at Themis Barbeque House through Swiggy's Dineout section for April 7, 2024 — ten guests from his account and four from his wife's. The listing showed "cost for two" as ₹1,500, implying ₹750 per person; the restaurant billed ₹1,050 per vegetarian buffet and ₹1,100 per non-vegetarian one — ₹300 and ₹350 more per head.

Singh also objected to a 10% service charge on beverages, raised it through Swiggy's in-app virtual chat, and got nowhere before approaching the commission (Consumer Complaint No. 8/DC/80/CC/422/2024). The restaurant never appeared despite being served and was proceeded against ex parte in February 2025.

Swiggy argued Dineout merely connects customers and restaurants, that "cost for two" was only an average signalling affordability, and invoked Section 79 of the IT Act, 2000. The bench rejected the shield: Section 79 protection is conditional on due diligence, and Swiggy showed none — no mechanism to reconcile displayed prices with actual billing. Under the 2022 Guidelines on Misleading Advertisements and the E-commerce Rules, 2020, the restaurant (owner of the advertisement) and the platform (its advertiser and host) were held equally responsible.

On the service charge, the menu neither disclosed the levy nor used the prescribed term "Staff Contribution," while the bill called it "Service Charge." Citing the Delhi High Court's ruling in National Restaurant Association of India v. Union of India, the commission held the levy a deficiency in service and unfair trade practice.

Impact & analysis

The precedent matters for platform-era dining: without an explicit estimate-or-average disclaimer, "cost for two" is a binding representation, and a 40%+ variance is misleading advertising under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 — not a rounding error.

The larger message is for every e-commerce platform: Section 79 of the IT Act is not blanket immunity. Intermediaries that profit from listings must show they verify them. It also lands amid wider scrutiny of dark patterns — a LocalCircles survey of 32,000 users found 68% had faced hidden charges on food-delivery apps, prompting calls for the Central Consumer Protection Authority to step in.

The diaspora angle

Swiggy Dineout is a staple for families visiting India — booking tables for large family dinners is exactly the use case here, a party of fourteen across two bookings. Returning NRIs carry the same protections as any local diner: screenshot the listing at booking time, and the platform shares liability if the bill doesn't match.

What's next

The four-week payment clock is running, with 12% annual interest thereafter. Both sides can appeal to the Delhi State Consumer Commission. Either way, expect "cost for two" labels to sprout "approximate" disclaimers soon — without one, the displayed number is now the promise.
